guideTitle: 6 Best Poultry Shears for Cutting Chicken Bones in 2026
metaDescription: Six poultry shears compared on blade thickness, steel hardness, spring assist and safety locks for spatchcocking chicken and cutting small bones.
introParagraphs: Poultry shears exist for one reason: a knife is awkward on a backbone, and ordinary kitchen scissors flex when they meet a rib or a wing joint. A proper pair has thicker blades, a stronger pivot, serrations that grip slippery skin and usually a spring that does the work of reopening the handles. Used well, they turn a whole chicken into spatchcocked halves in a minute or two.

We evaluated six distinct pairs from a crowded category, spanning the OXO Good Grips curved spring-loaded design, the MAD SHARK with 3.5mm blades, the HeesHoos at 54 HRC, the TUOLEWE with a bone-holding groove and the LIBERHAUS at 9.4 inches. The comparison uses product specs and buyer feedback on each listing, not a lab test, and it focuses on the things that decide bone performance: blade thickness, steel hardness, serration, spring and lock design, and how easily the pair comes clean after raw poultry.

Thickness and hardness pull in opposite directions. A thicker blade resists flexing against cartilage, while a harder steel holds an edge but can chip if you twist against bone. The best pair for your kitchen sits where your cutting habits do.

products.name: MAD SHARK Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The MAD SHARK combines the main features a poultry shear needs. It uses rust-resistant molybdenum-vanadium steel, precision-tempered blades that are 3.5mm thick and spring-loaded handles that reopen after every squeeze. A thumb-activated lock holds the blades closed for storage.

The 3.5mm blade is the number to focus on for bones. It is thick enough to stay rigid against a backbone or a drumstick joint, and the listing describes a one-handed lock designed for quick operation. The maker also mentions a built-in nut cracker, which turns it into a holiday-season all-rounder. Because it is a dedicated poultry tool, it is heavier and bulkier than a normal kitchen scissor.

In ownership terms, expect to store it in a drawer or block with the lock on, and expect to clean the pivot carefully after raw chicken. Compared with the TUOLEWE at 3.0mm it has a thicker blade, and compared with the HeesHoos it matches the 3.5mm spec but adds a stated lock and steel type. It is the most complete package in this lineup.
products.bestFor: Cooks who spatchcock chicken and turkey regularly.
pros: 3.5mm blades stay rigid on bones and joints
Spring-loaded handles reduce hand fatigue
Thumb lock for quick one-handed closing
Molybdenum-vanadium steel resists rust
cons: Spring and lock add parts that can wear

products.name: OXO Good Grips Spring-Loaded Poultry Shears
products.description:
The OXO shears take a different approach with curved, tapered blades designed to reach hard-to-access spots near the cavity. The stainless steel micro-serrated edges are notched to hold bones in place, which stops them from sliding away mid-cut. Spring-loaded handles reduce the effort of repeated cuts.

The curved shape helps when you cut along a backbone or trim around a thigh joint, because the blade tip follows the contour of the bird. The blades separate for cleaning, which the listing says can be done by hand or in the dishwasher, and that is a real benefit after raw poultry. The listing does not publish a blade thickness, so you cannot compare the thickness directly with the 3.5mm MAD SHARK.

In practice this is the easiest pair to clean, which matters if you cook poultry often. Next to the LIBERHAUS at 9.4 inches, the OXO is more about control than length. It is a good fit for cooks who value cleaning and reach over a stated hardness rating.

products.name: HeesHoos Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The HeesHoos pair is forged from food-grade stainless steel with a stated Rockwell hardness of 54 plus or minus 2. The blade is 3.5mm thick, matching the MAD SHARK, and the spring-loaded design is meant for chicken, turkey and a range of everyday cuts.

Stating both hardness and thickness is rare in this category. A figure around 54 HRC sits in a sensible range for shears that need to hold an edge without chipping on bone. The handles are described as suitable for a wide range of hand sizes, which helps if several people share the tool.

The tradeoff is that the listing does not mention a lock in the excerpt we reviewed, so you should check the product page before buying if storage safety is important. In use it competes directly with the MAD SHARK on thickness and offers published hardness where the MAD SHARK gives steel type. It suits buyers who like to see the numbers.

products.description:
The TUOLEWE scissors use 420J2 stainless steel with 3.0mm thickened blades. The maker compares these to the 2.0mm to 2.5mm blades of everyday kitchen shears and says the extra thickness prevents bending.

A built-in groove acts as a holder for bones, herbs and tough ingredients, which stops them from slipping while you cut. That small design touch helps with control and safety on small bones. The blade is thicker than a standard pair but thinner than the 3.5mm MAD SHARK and HeesHoos, so it sits between a kitchen scissor and a full poultry shear.

In use it suits cooks who want one sturdy pair for chicken, herbs and general tasks rather than a specialist tool. It is likely a good fit for wings, thighs and small joints rather than whole turkey backbones, where the thicker pairs have the edge. Check the listing for handle shape before ordering, since the excerpt does not describe it.

products.name: SLEMOON Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The SLEMOON shears are forged stainless steel with a micro-serrated edge that grips wet, slippery skin. Spring-loaded handles let you cut through a backbone with one hand, and a safety lock holds the blades closed for storage.

The unique part is the spare spring packed in the box. A worn or lost spring is one of the typical failure points for this style, and having a replacement means you can keep using the tool instead of replacing it. The listing mentions 3.5 inch blades, a riveted fishbone handle and a burgundy finish.

This is a practical choice if you cook poultry for holidays and want a tool that can be repaired. The listing does not give a blade thickness in millimeters, so compare it to the MAD SHARK on thickness only after checking the product page. It is a strong choice for cooks who think about long-term ownership.

products.name: LIBERHAUS Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The LIBERHAUS shears measure 9.4 inches and use rust-resistant 3CR14 steel with a serrated edge that helps grip joints. They are spring-loaded with a safety lock, and the listing describes them as made for poultry prep and joint cutting.

The longer handle gives extra leverage, which can help on small bones and wing joints. The 3CR14 steel is a common, mid-range stainless that is easy to maintain and resharpen. The listing says the tool gives controlled bone cutting for small bones rather than heavy thick bones.

Compared with the MAD SHARK at 3.5mm it is a lighter-duty option, but it brings more length and a lock. Against the OXO it has less cleaning convenience and no curved blade. It suits cooks who want leverage and a lock in a conventional shape.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Thicker blades resist flexing when they meet cartilage and bone. Guides commonly suggest around 3.5mm at the spine for poultry work, and the MAD SHARK and HeesHoos both list exactly that. The TUOLEWE sits at 3.0mm, which is stronger than the 2.0mm to 2.5mm of everyday kitchen shears but a step below. If a listing gives no thickness, as with the OXO and LIBERHAUS, check the product page before expecting bone performance. Thicker blades also weigh more, so the MAD SHARK will feel heavier than the TUOLEWE during a long prep session.

Hardness around 53 to 57 HRC balances edge retention and chip resistance, and anything much below 50 HRC tends to dull quickly. The HeesHoos publishes 54 plus or minus 2 HRC, which is useful transparency. The TUOLEWE uses 420J2 and the LIBERHAUS uses 3CR14, both common stainless grades. Harder steel holds an edge but can chip if you twist against bone, so cut straight along the line of the bone. If you only cut chicken thighs and wings, you do not need to chase the highest hardness figure, since a sharp 3CR14 blade does the job.

A spring reopens the handles after every cut, which cuts hand effort during a whole-bird breakdown. A safety lock keeps the blades closed in the drawer. The MAD SHARK, SLEMOON and LIBERHAUS all list a lock. Check that the spring does not jam when the handles are fully closed, since some designs can lock up if squeezed hard. A stiff spring tires the hand just like a manual pair, so read buyer feedback on how much force the handles need to close.

Curved and tapered blades follow the contour of a bird and reach into tight spots near the cavity. The OXO uses this design, while the others are straighter. Straight blades give more direct force along a backbone. Pick curved for control and straight for raw power. Curved blades can feel less direct on a thick turkey backbone, where the straighter pairs push force along the line of the cut.

Raw poultry leaves residue at the pivot, so cleaning design matters. The OXO blades separate for hand or dishwasher cleaning. Fixed pivots such as the MAD SHARK rely on thorough washing and careful drying. Follow USDA guidance for tools that touch raw poultry. Brush the pivot, rinse well and let the blades dry open so moisture does not sit in the joint overnight.

Serrations stop wet skin and bones from sliding while you cut. The OXO has notches designed to hold bones in place, the TUOLEWE has a built-in groove, and the SLEMOON and LIBERHAUS use serrated edges. Better grip means safer cuts and fewer slips. Dull blades push you to hack, which raises the risk of a slip, so keep the edge sharp. Keep the grooves and notches clear of bone chips, since packed debris reduces grip on the next cut.

faq.q: What are the best poultry shears for chicken bones?
faq.a: For bones the MAD SHARK and HeesHoos stand out with 3.5mm blades. The MAD SHARK adds a thumb lock and stated steel type. The HeesHoos publishes a hardness of 54 plus or minus 2 HRC. Either is a strong choice for backbones and joints. Pick the thickness to match your toughest recurring task.

faq.q: How thick should poultry shears be?
faq.a: Guides commonly suggest around 3.5mm at the spine for poultry work, since thinner blades flex against cartilage and joints. The MAD SHARK and HeesHoos meet that figure. The TUOLEWE at 3.0mm is a step below. Everyday kitchen shears at 2.0mm to 2.5mm are not meant for bones. Keep the lock on whenever the shears are stored, and keep a spare spring if the pair offers one.

faq.q: Are spring-loaded poultry shears worth it?
faq.a: A spring reopens the handles after each cut, which reduces hand effort during a whole-bird breakdown. The MAD SHARK, OXO, SLEMOON and LIBERHAUS use springs. Check that the spring does not lock up when fully closed. A spare spring such as the one in the SLEMOON box adds peace of mind. If you want one pair for a holiday turkey, choose a 3.5mm model with a lock.

faq.q: How do I spatchcock a chicken with shears?
faq.a: Cut along both sides of the backbone and stay tight to the spine. Remove the backbone, then press on the breastbone until the bird flattens. Common mistakes include cutting the breastbone instead of the backbone and using dull shears. A sharp pair makes the cut straight and safe. Rest the bird on a stable board and keep fingers clear of the blade path.

faq.q: How do I clean poultry shears?
faq.a: Wash them with hot soapy water or use the dishwasher if the listing allows it. Separable blades like the OXO are easiest to clean. Dry the pivot fully to prevent rust. Follow USDA guidance for tools that touch raw poultry. A small brush helps reach the pivot and the serrated edge.

faq.q: Can I use poultry shears for other food?
faq.a: Yes. Most poultry shears also cut herbs, packaging and vegetables. The TUOLEWE and MAD SHARK both mention multi-purpose use. A heavy pair is bulkier than normal scissors, so keep a lighter pair for daily tasks. Keep a lighter pair for daily jobs so the poultry shears stay sharp for bones.

Eventually. Stainless steels like 3CR14 on the LIBERHAUS are easy to resharpen, while harder steels hold an edge longer. Serrated edges are harder to sharpen at home. Gentle washing and drying help the edge last. A food-safe oil on the pivot after drying keeps a spring pair moving smoothly.
